comments.text: Three pages of glyphs beginning at $0800. The score screen selects this character RAM through $D018.
Four pages of authored score-screen cells copied to $0400 before the name and number overlays.

Installs a VIC-II preset, selects the $0800 character generator, and runs score insertion before drawing the scores and starting the screen's sound. Waits on a CIA1 port A reading of $6F before muting the SID and leaving via $C900.
Sets the KERNAL input and output device numbers to 0 and 3. Copies the VIC-II preset from $ECB9, leaving display control, border and background colour unchanged.

Scans five twelve-byte records by unsigned score, comparing the high byte first. A new score equal to or above a record takes its position. The copy beginning at $C297 shifts twelve-byte slots up in memory before the ten-character name and score are written into the selected slot.
Splits the two-byte binary score in $C699/$C69A into four nibbles. Uses each nibble to choose a decimal place contribution and adds them into the five output digits.
Adds the five digits addressed by the patched operand at $C3F1 to the output at $C69B. On a sum of ten or more, writes the digit modulo ten and carries one into the next position.
Calls the KERNAL with device 8, secondary address zero and the name H. Requests the destination $C868 in X and Y.
Saves the five 12-byte score records from $C868 through $C8A3. Supplies the replacement filename @:H and the exclusive end address $C8A4.
At raster $FF, sets border and background to black and blanks the display. Returns after 100 successful reads of raster line zero.
Copies the four-page score matrix from $1000 into screen RAM. Sets colour RAM based on the copied character codes and selects multicolour character mode.
Indexes the message sequence list, drawing each entry through $C513 until $FF.
Uses row and column from the selected message to address screen RAM, converts its letters to screen codes and handles $FE for another row and $FF for the end.
Masks CIA1 interrupt sources and selects RAM under the KERNAL. Calls $E003 to initialize the tune and installs the hardware IRQ vector at $C5B7.
Acknowledges the VIC-II raster IRQ, preserves A, X, Y and the sound player scratch at $FA–$FF, and calls the player at $E000. Restores the compare to line zero.
Twenty-five little-endian multiples of 40. The message renderer adds the selected row offset and the message column to $0400.
Pointer selected by A=0 at $C4EB. It addresses the message list at $C631.
Selects message zero and ends with $FF.
Pointer to message zero, the five score rows.

Five rows at column 13, starting on screen rows $0C, $0E, $10, $12 and $14. Score insertion and formatting fill each row with a ten-character name and five decimal digits. $FE starts another row and $FF ends the message.
Little-endian score copied from one record at a time for the four nibble lookups in the decimal formatter.
Five PETSCII digits initialized to zero by $C36C. The formatter accumulates the string contributions of the four nibbles here before copying the result into the message rows.
Lookup for the low nibble of the low score byte, with 16 pointers to five-digit decimal strings.
Lookup for the high nibble of the low score byte, indexing its decimal contribution in multiples of 16.
Lookup for the low nibble of the high score byte, indexing its decimal contribution in multiples of 256.
Lookup for the high nibble of the high score byte, indexing its decimal contribution in multiples of 4096.
Sixteen five-digit decimal strings for values zero through fifteen.
Sixteen five-digit decimal strings for values zero through 240 in steps of 16.
Sixteen five-digit decimal strings for values zero through 3840 in steps of 256.
Sixteen five-digit decimal strings for values zero through 61440 in steps of 4096.
Four scratch offsets written by the decimal formatter, one for each score nibble. Each offset selects a two-byte pointer to the five-digit contribution.
The three-byte replacement name @:H used for SAVE, followed by the one-byte name H used for LOAD.
Five records of 12 bytes. Each holds a ten-character name and a two-byte score, compared most-significant byte first before insertion.
The insertion copy at $C29A reads the first ten bytes of this area and can write through $C8B9. These bytes sit after the five records and outside the 60-byte span saved under @:H.
Blanks the screen, restores the ROM mapping, installs the RAM LOAD vector and calls SETLFS for device 8 before choosing the next file.
The five characters LABLE passed to SETNAM at $C91C before loading the title program.
Clears or sets $CE01, $CE24 and $CE02 from A, then calls the BASIC CLR and RUN entries with A=0. The active score exit jumps to BASIC RUN from $C929 before this sequence.
A second copy of the five-character name LABLE after the alternate BASIC call sequence. The score exit uses the copy at $C92C.
IRQ entry for the score music. Jumps to $E0AF to service the voices.
Clears the voice runtime state at $E6CF–$E728 and resets the SID register set. Uses the tune index in A to install six initial voice pointers and the tempo byte.
Decodes negative values fetched from a voice sequence. $FF replaces the sequence pointer from the next two bytes. Other command ranges write per-voice properties at $E714, $E717 or $E70B.
Starts with voice index 2 and checks the voice timers before fetching the next note or command. Uses the sign bit of the initializer-patched operand at $E0B2 to force the sequence-fetch path.

Uses the phrase index for this voice to select a pointer from $E729, then reads the byte at the current phrase position. For values below $60, adds the voice offset at $E714 and stores the resulting note index.
Decrements the voice index to service the next voice. After the last voice it updates the driver timer and its global SID settings.
Uses the active instrument and per-voice selectors to choose a waveform sequence, apply its wait and loop fields and update the note and pitch offsets.

Updates the pulse accumulator using timed eight-bit step commands selected by the instrument. Chooses the control byte from the instrument or a control sequence and masks it against voice state before writing the SID registers.
Saves X, looks up the instrument envelope bytes by the active voice instrument and writes SID attack/decay and sustain/release at offsets $D405 and $D406. Restores X and advances the voice.
Instrument parameter bytes indexed by the instrument offset held at $E6D8 per voice. The player draws the envelope, waveform, pulse sequence and control settings from successive fields.
Split pointer, length and loop data read at $E387–$E399. The driver writes the selected override into the first slot of each table at $E35E–$E370.
Split low and high pointer tables for the timed pulse-step streams. $E47A and $E47F fetch the pointer selected by the low five bits of the instrument setting.
Split pointers and restart indices for control-byte sequences. The instrument selects the sequence and supplies its length at $E4AD.
Small parameter tables indexed by the player at $E24C, $E251 and $E144. $E144 puts the selected value into the individual voice state.
Four four-byte tables for the per-voice waveform override. $E35B–$E370 copies the chosen pointer, length and loop index into the waveform directory.
Bytes before the low frequency table. The pitch-step calculation at $E400 can use its last entry through the indexed operand $E60D,Y.
Two 95-byte arrays starting at $E60E and $E66D. The player uses the note index to read the low and high bytes of the SID frequency word.
SID voice register offsets 0, 7 and 14 used to select the active voice register group.
Sixteen pointers to song phrases. The doubled pattern number held in the current voice position at $E70E selects the pointer.
The score song supplies three low and three high bytes of voice sequence addresses. Initialization copies them into the current pointers at $E705–$E70A.
The tune setup copies this byte to the immediate operand at $E22E.
Waveform, pulse-step and control sequences addressed by the player directories at $E58E–$E5DE. Pulse data includes a delay and a step, with a high-bit command to jump back within the stream.
Initial track for SID voice 1. Pattern numbers select phrases through $E729 and $FF followed by a word loops the track back to its start.
Initial track for SID voice 2. Pattern numbers select phrases through $E729 and $FF followed by a word loops the track back to its start.
Initial track for SID voice 3. Pattern numbers select phrases through $E729 and $FF followed by a word loops the track back to its start.
Music phrase data at the pointer for pattern 0. The phrase reader at $E0D1 fetches these note and control bytes through a zero-page pointer.
